source.title: The Dual-Route Model of Induction
source.authors: Sheridan Feucht; Eric Todd; Byron C. Wallace; David Bau

record.tranche_reason: Uses causal activation patching, attention measurements and head ablations to test copying behavior, rather than the original training-time/loss measurements.
record.gate_note: The paper measures token- and concept-copying heads, their attention patterns, and effects of ablating them. It also measures copying-head scores across checkpoints for OLMo-2-7b and Pythia-6.9b. It does not measure loss by token index, an in-context-learning gain, or a training-loss bump. Detailed results for language-pair translation patching and many task-specific ablation curves are not included as rows because they do not directly measure the claim versions.
record.test_reason: Uses causal patching, next-token attention scores and mean-ablation in pretrained 1B–8B LLMs. Token induction heads are identified and shown to be needed for verbatim copying across four families, which bears on V4. Token-head ablation leaves semantic in-context list tasks intact while FV-head ablation does not, which bears narrowly on V6. There are no small attention-only models, no loss-by-token-index measure and no measure of abrupt formation.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also stress three points: the two routes operate independently; ablating token induction heads makes models paraphrase rather than copy verbatim; FV heads complement concept heads by carrying output-language information during translation.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses pretrained language models, causal patching, attention matching, and targeted head ablations to study copying. It does not reproduce the original small-transformer training setup or use the original loss-by-token-index and training-loss-bump measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: The degree of separation between token- and concept-head effects differs by model: Pythia-6.9b is less clear-cut, and the authors also report overlap between head types in OLMo-2-7b. Checkpoint patterns differ between OLMo-2-7b and Pythia-6.9b.

fits_no_version.finding: Concept induction heads attend to the last token of multi-token words and copy whole lexical units. They are separate from token induction heads and are needed for translation, synonym and antonym tasks across models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: LLMs have a second, concept-level induction route that runs in parallel with token induction heads.

fits_no_version.finding: In OLMo-2-7b, some top concept induction heads have high token-copying scores early in training before becoming concept heads. The pattern is unclear in Pythia-6.9b.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Concept induction heads may develop from token induction heads during training.

record.problems: Training trajectories are shown for only OLMo-2-7b and Pythia-6.9b, without numerical checkpoint values stated in the text. The comparison of training-token counts across model families does not isolate training setup as a cause. Many task-ablation results are presented in figures rather than numerically in the text.
record.rows_left_out: Detailed layer/head score plots and the full task-specific ablation curves in Figures 3–5 and 9–18, 23–38 were not transcribed as separate rows where the text provides no separate numeric result. Language-pair activation-patching results in Figures 6–7 and 45–47 are not direct tests of the listed versions.

untested.parts: Small attention-only transformers and K-composition with a previous-token head are not tested. All models are large pretrained LLMs.
Abruptness, timing window, co-occurring ICL gain and loss bump are all untested. The checkpoint figures give no such measures.
Loss by token index and the share of ICL due to induction heads are not measured.
Other architectures and modalities, and multiple training runs of the same model, are not tested.
No manipulation of data or training setup. The Pythia token-count explanation is speculative.
Only vocabulary-list copying, translation, synonym and antonym tasks are tested, not general few-shot ICL benchmarks.
Sub-steps of induction-head formation are not measured.

missing.what: Ablating top-k FV heads strongly damages the non-verbatim vocabulary-list tasks.
Token-copying vs next-token-matching correlations for each model other than Llama-2-7b (described only as significant).
OLMo-2-1b copying scores and ablation results, covering a smaller size.
missing.locator: Appendix A Figs 15–16; Appendix D Fig 36

missing.what: Token-head ablation of k=32 heads causes paraphrasing instead of verbatim copying; Pythia's paraphrases are poorer.

record.verdict_notes: V1 links were removed because the study uses large pretrained LLMs, not small attention-only models, and never tests previous-token composition. The V6 bearing is narrow. The concept induction heads are themselves a kind of induction head, so the result says verbatim token induction heads are not needed for these semantic list tasks; it does not show that induction-style heads in general are uninvolved. The authors cite Yin & Steinhardt (2025) on FV heads but do not test general few-shot ICL. Checkpoint figures give no numbers. The tranche could arguably be T3, as a new setting.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test small attention-only transformers or whether induction heads form by composing with an earlier previous-token head. Tests token-copying behavior and the effects of ablating identified token-copying heads in pretrained models.

Checkpoint measurements address head-score trajectories only. The study does not test whether formation is abrupt in a narrow window, whether it coincides with an in-context-learning gain, or whether that gain appears as a training-loss bump.
Does not measure most in-context learning, loss falling with token index, or induction-head contributions to that behavior in large transformers.
Tests several pretrained language-model families and sizes, but not other architectures or modalities, or the breadth of training runs implied by universality.

Compares models with different stated training-token counts and reports checkpoint trajectories for two models, but does not manipulate data or setup while holding other factors fixed, and does not measure whether in-context learning persists.
Does not test few-shot task learning as distinct from copying. Function-vector heads are discussed and tested in translation experiments, but not as an explanation of most few-shot learning.
Checkpoint trajectories are shown for two models, but the study does not test whether the original induction-head/ICL/loss transition comprises multiple separate transitions.

rows.subject: all four models evaluated on vocabulary-list ablations

conditions.value: translation, synonyms, antonyms, and surface-level tasks

rows.value: For all models, concept-head ablation damages semantic tasks more than surface-level tasks; Pythia shows less separation between the roles.
rows.note: Aggregate qualitative result as stated by the authors. Pythia’s weaker separation is reported in r8.
rows.check: Concept-head ablation is not a standard induction-head measure. The record's state 'partial' misreads the result: the effect is reported for all models. Belongs in fits_no_version.

rows.subject: Pythia-6.9b
rows.value: Unlike the other models, token-head ablation also damages semantic tasks; capitalization and English-copying accuracy remain relatively high.
rows.note: The authors suggest the model's training on an order of magnitude fewer tokens than the others may be related to token and concept induction being more fused; this comparison does not isolate training-token count.
rows.check: In Pythia, token-head ablation also damages semantic tasks, so token induction heads carry part of the semantic list tasks here (partial for V6). For V5 it should be cannot_determine: the training-token explanation is the authors' speculation, confounded by model family.

source_check.correct: V6: partial. V4: cannot_determine from semantic-task damage alone. V5: cannot_determine; the proposed explanation involving 0.3 trillion training tokens is tentative and the comparison does not isolate training-data effects.
